Long chat or new chat? What 30 requests cost in Claude Code

Measured and written by Jonhisking · Updated 2026-10-23. Disclosure: TokenSave gets no funding, credits or sponsorship from AI companies. All measurements use our own paid subscriptions.

Starting a new chat for every request cost 129% more than staying in one long chat. We sent the same 30 change requests to one browser game in Claude Code three ways. One long session cost $4.16 on average, one session with /compact halfway $4.70 (+13%), and a fresh session for every request $9.52 (+129%).

Measured 2026-10-20 · Claude Code (Opus 5.5) · 30 requests × 3 strategies × 2 runs · License CC BY 4.0

DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23489464 · Also on Hugging Face · Kaggle · GitHub

Key findings

  • A new session per request was the most expensive strategy, by far. Total API cost: one session $4.05 and $4.27; a new session each time $9.19 and $9.84. Both runs agree.
  • Why: a fresh session has to find its way back in. Without the conversation, Claude Code re-read the game file and rebuilt its prompt cache on every request: a mean of 6.7 model calls and 29,178 newly cached tokens per request, against 5.2 calls and 4,061 in the long session. A one-hour cache write costs 100% more than normal input; a cache read costs 95% less.
  • A long chat does get more expensive per message. In one session, requests 2–5 cost $0.029 each on average and requests 26–30 cost $0.284, +868%, because every message re-reads a longer history and the game kept growing. Even then, a late message in the long chat was cheaper than a late message in a fresh session ($0.435).
  • /compact did not save money here. Compacting after request 15 cost $0.11 and $0.11 itself, and the next request had to rebuild the cache, so the total came out +13% against the uncompacted session. Over 30 requests the shorter history never paid that back.
  • All six final games worked after 30 rounds of changes, whichever strategy was used.

Results by strategy

Two runs each. Per-request costs are means over both runs. For one-session strategies Claude Code reports session totals, so each request is the difference from the previous one; the cost of the /compact call is counted in the total. Cost is the API list-price estimate (Opus 5.5).

What to take from it

  • For a run of related changes to the same project, keep going in the same session; that is what the prompt cache is built for.
  • Start a new session when you switch to unrelated work, not between every small change.
  • Save /compact for when the context is close to full or the history is confusing the model. It is not a cost-saving step on its own.
  • Pauses matter too: the cache only lasts so long, which is the subject of our coffee-break measurement.

Method

  • Claude Code 2.1.295 with Opus 5.5 on one Windows laptop, claude -p --effort medium --permission-mode acceptEdits, no MCP servers. Request 1 builds a brick-breaker game; requests 2–30 change it (ball colour, levels, sound, touch controls, a clean-up at the end). The full list is in the JSON download.
  • One session: requests 2–30 sent with --resume to the first session. /compact: the same, with /compact sent after request 15. New session: each request in a new session in the same folder, prefixed with “The game is in index.html in the current folder.”.
  • All three strategies ran at the same time, twice, on 2026-10-20. Tokens and cost from the result event of each call.

Limitations

  • One project of about 30–40 KB and requests that mostly touch the same file. A long session that wanders across unrelated work, or one that reaches the context limit and auto-compacts, may behave differently.
  • Claude Code only. Other tools cache differently.
  • On a subscription the bill does not change, but the same difference applies to how fast you reach the usage limit.
